title: Δόλων καὶ Ῥῆσος
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Trembling, Dolon answers Odysseus: Hector led him astray with a promise of Achilles’ horses and sent him to learn whether the ships are guarded. Odysseus smiles and asks where Hector is, where his gear and horses lie, and how the Trojan watches are set. Dolon says Hector is in council by the tomb of Ilus, that the Trojans keep their own fires but the summoned allies sleep, and he lists the allies by where they lie. He points the two spies to the newly arrived Thracians and their king Rhesus, whose horses are whiter than snow and run like the winds, and whose golden armour is fit for a god, and begs to be bound or taken to the ships. Diomedes will not let him go, and as Dolon reaches to beg he strikes through his neck. They strip the body, Odysseus dedicates the spoils to Athena on a tamarisk, and they find the Thracians asleep in rows with Rhesus in the middle; Odysseus points him out and tells Diomedes either to loose the horses or to kill the men while he sees to the horses.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Δόλων, ὑπὸ δ’ ἔτρεμε γυῖα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Dolōn, hypo d’ etreme guia·
sentences.l: Him then answered Dolon, and beneath trembled his limbs:
sentences.i: Then Dolon answered him, and his limbs trembled beneath him:
sentences.n: The reply formula τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ‘him then answered’, with Dolon as the speaker; the edition begins a new paragraph here, and Odysseus’ last question (‘did your own heart urge you on?’) is what Dolon is answering. ὑπὸ δ’ ἔτρεμε is a tmesis of ὑποτρέμω ‘tremble beneath’, an imperfect, and its subject γυῖα ‘limbs’ is a neuter plural with a singular verb, which Greek allows.

sentences.t:
πολλῇσίν μ’ ἄτῃσι παρὲκ νόον ἤγαγεν Ἕκτωρ,
ὅς μοι Πηλεΐωνος ἀγαυοῦ μώνυχας ἵππους
δωσέμεναι κατένευσε καὶ ἅρματα ποικίλα χαλκῷ,
sentences.tr:
pollēisin m’ atēisi parek noon ēgagen Hektōr,
hos moi Pēleïōnos agauou mōnychas hippous
dōsemenai kateneuse kai harmata poikila chalkōi,
sentences.l:
“With many bewilderments beyond my mind led me Hector,
who to me of Peleus’-son, the noble, the solid-hoofed horses
to give nodded assent, and the chariot intricate with bronze,
sentences.i: “Hector has led me out of my wits with many bewilderments; he nodded his assent to give me the solid-hoofed horses of the noble son of Peleus, and the chariot intricately worked with bronze,
sentences.n: Dolon puts the blame on Hector. ἄτῃσι is the dative plural of ἄτη, the house ‘bewilderment’, and παρὲκ νόον ἤγαγεν is ‘led me out past my mind’, παρέκ taking the accusative. Πηλεΐωνος is the genitive of Πηλεΐων, a patronymic form of Πηλεύς, ‘Peleus’-son’, which here means Achilles; ἀγαυοῦ is ‘noble’. μώνυχας ἵππους is the house ‘solid-hoofed horses’. δωσέμεναι is a future infinitive in -μεναι, ‘to give’, depending on κατένευσε ‘nodded assent’, the nod being the sign of a promise. ἅρματα is a plural for the one chariot, and ποικίλα χαλκῷ is ‘intricate with bronze’.

sentences.t:
ἠνώγει δέ μ’ ἰόντα θοὴν διὰ νύκτα μέλαιναν
ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων σχεδὸν ἐλθέμεν, ἔκ τε πυθέσθαι
ἠὲ φυλάσσονται νῆες θοαὶ ὡς τὸ πάρος περ,
sentences.tr:
ēnōgei de m’ ionta thoēn dia nykta melainan
andrōn dysmeneōn schedon elthemen, ek te pythesthai
ēe phylassontai nēes thoai hōs to paros per,
sentences.l:
and he bade me, going through the swift black night,
to come near to hostile men, and to find out
whether the swift ships are guarded as before,
sentences.i: and he bade me go through the swift black night, come near the hostile men, and find out whether the swift ships are guarded just as before,
sentences.n: Dolon gives Hector’s orders, in almost Hector’s own words (compare 10.308–309 in the last part). ἠνώγει is the pluperfect of ἄνωγα used as a past, ‘he bade’, and it governs two infinitives, ἐλθέμεν ‘to come’ (-έμεν = -ειν) and ἔκ … πυθέσθαι ‘to find out’, a tmesis for ἐκπυθέσθαι; ἰόντα ‘going’ agrees with μ’ ‘me’. θοὴν … νύκτα μέλαιναν is ‘the swift black night’: θοός is the stock ‘swift’, kept even of night. ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων ‘hostile men’ depends on σχεδόν ‘near’. ἠέ … ‘whether’ opens a double question that ἦ in 397 completes.

sentences.t:
ἦ ἤδη χείρεσσιν ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃσι δαμέντες
φύξιν βουλεύουσι μετὰ σφίσιν, οὐδ’ ἐθέλουσι
νύκτα φυλασσέμεναι, καμάτῳ ἀδηκότες αἰνῷ.
sentences.tr:
ē ēdē cheiressin hyph’ hēmeterēisi damentes
phyxin bouleuousi meta sphisin, oud’ ethelousi
nykta phylassemenai, kamatōi adēkotes ainōi.
sentences.l:
or whether, already beneath our hands overcome,
they are planning flight among themselves, and are unwilling
to keep watch through the night, worn out with fearsome weariness.”
sentences.i: or whether, overcome already beneath our hands, they are plotting flight among themselves and do not want to keep watch in the night, worn out by fearsome weariness.”
sentences.n: These three lines are word for word 10.310–312 of the last part, where Hector set Dolon his task, and they take the English they have there. ἦ is ‘or whether’, answering ἠέ in 396, and not ‘truly’. δαμέντες is the aorist passive participle of δαμάζω ‘overcome’, with χείρεσσιν ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃσι ‘beneath our hands’, and ἀδηκότες is the house ‘worn out’ (the sense is not quite certain). Dolon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἐπιμειδήσας προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ epimeidēsas prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him then smiling at addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles, smiling at him, spoke to him:
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph, and Odysseus replies. This is the formula τὸν δ’ ἐπιμειδήσας προσέφη ‘him then smiling at addressed’, which the Odyssey has for Odysseus at 22.371, and it takes that English. ἐπιμειδήσας is the aorist participle of ἐπιμειδάω ‘smile at’, and πολύμητις is the house epithet ‘of many wiles’ (μῆτις is ‘cunning’).

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥά νύ τοι μεγάλων δώρων ἐπεμαίετο θυμὸς
ἵππων Αἰακίδαο δαΐφρονος·
sentences.tr:
ē rha ny toi megalōn dōrōn epemaieto thymos
hippōn Aiakidao daïphronos·
sentences.l:
“Truly then, now, of great gifts was reaching your heart,
of the horses of Aeacus’ descendant, the wise-minded;
sentences.i: “So your heart was reaching, then, for great gifts, the horses of the wise-hearted descendant of Aeacus:
sentences.n: Odysseus’ tone is sharp. ἦ ῥά νύ is ‘truly, then, now’, and τοι is the dative ‘to you’, here with θυμός as ‘your heart’ (it could also be the particle ‘I tell you’). ἐπεμαίετο is the imperfect of ἐπιμαίομαι ‘reach after’, and it takes the genitive μεγάλων δώρων ‘great gifts’, which the next words explain: ἵππων Αἰακίδαο ‘the horses of Aeacus’ descendant’, that is Achilles. δαΐφρονος is the house ‘wise-minded’; whether the word means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed. The unit ends at the raised dot in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀλεγεινοὶ
ἀνδράσι γε θνητοῖσι δαμήμεναι ἠδ’ ὀχέεσθαι
ἄλλῳ γ’ ἢ Ἀχιλῆϊ, τὸν ἀθανάτη τέκε μήτηρ.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ alegeinoi
andrasi ge thnētoisi damēmenai ēd’ ocheesthai
allōi g’ ē Achilēï, ton athanatē teke mētēr.
sentences.i: and they are grievous for mortal men, at least, to tame and to drive, for any but Achilles, whom an immortal mother bore.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, the horses: in Homer a word that looks like a relative is often a demonstrative. ἀλεγεινοί is the house ‘grievous’, here ‘troublesome, hard to handle’, and it takes two infinitives, δαμήμεναι ‘to be tamed’ (the aorist passive of δαμάζω, the verb that means ‘overcome’ when it is said of men, as in 397 and 411) and ὀχέεσθαι, from ὀχέομαι ‘be carried, ride’, which said of the team means being driven. ἀνδράσι γε θνητοῖσι is ‘for mortal men, at least’, and ἄλλῳ γ’ ἢ Ἀχιλῆϊ ‘for any other than Achilles’. ἀθανάτη is the feminine of ἀθάνατος ‘immortal’ (the same form for both genders), and τέκε is an unaugmented aorist, ‘bore’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον·
sentences.tr: all’ age moi tode eipe kai atrekeōs katalexon·
sentences.l: But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly;
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly:
sentences.n: This line stands word for word at 10.384 in the last part and takes the English it has there. ἀλλ’ ἄγε ‘but come’ opens a command; εἰπέ is the aorist imperative ‘tell’, and κατάλεξον the aorist imperative of καταλέγω ‘recount’. ἀτρεκέως is ‘exactly’, and Dolon promises it back when he answers (413).

sentences.t: ποῦ νῦν δεῦρο κιὼν λίπες Ἕκτορα ποιμένα λαῶν;
sentences.tr: pou nyn deuro kiōn lipes Hektora poimena laōn;
sentences.l: Where now, coming here, did you leave Hector, shepherd of the people?
sentences.i: Where did you leave Hector, shepherd of the people, when you came here?
sentences.n: Odysseus now puts a run of questions to Dolon (406–411). ποῦ is ‘where’, κιών the present participle of κίω ‘go’ (‘coming’) with δεῦρο ‘here’, and λίπες an unaugmented aorist, ‘you left’. ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is the stock title of a leader.

sentences.t: ποῦ δέ οἱ ἔντεα κεῖται ἀρήϊα, ποῦ δέ οἱ ἵπποι;
sentences.tr: pou de hoi entea keitai arēïa, pou de hoi hippoi;
sentences.l: And where lies his warlike gear, and where are his horses?
sentences.i: And where does his warlike gear lie, and where are his horses?
sentences.n: οἱ is the dative ‘his’ (‘for him’), used twice. ἔντεα is the house ‘gear’, kept apart from τεύχεα ‘armour’, and ἀρήϊα is ‘warlike’.

sentences.t: πῶς δαὶ τῶν ἄλλων Τρώων φυλακαί τε καὶ εὐναί;
sentences.tr: pōs dai tōn allōn Trōōn phylakai te kai eunai;
sentences.l: And how, then, of the other Trojans are the watches and the beds?
sentences.i: And how stand the watches and the sleeping-places of the rest of the Trojans?
sentences.n: πῶς δαί is ‘how, then?’; δαί is a particle that sharpens a question. φυλακαί ‘watches’ (house) are the guard-duties, and εὐναί ‘beds’ (the plural of εὐνή) are the places where men sleep. Dolon answers them at 414–422.

sentences.t:
ἅσσά τε μητιόωσι μετὰ σφίσιν, ἢ μεμάασιν
αὖθι μένειν παρὰ νηυσὶν ἀπόπροθεν, ἦε πόλιν δὲ
ἂψ ἀναχωρήσουσιν, ἐπεὶ δαμάσαντό γ’ Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr:
hassa te mētioōsi meta sphisin, ē memaasin
authi menein para nēusin apoprothen, ēe polin de
aps anachōrēsousin, epei damasanto g’ Achaious.
sentences.l:
and what things they are devising among themselves, or are eager
to stay here by the ships, far off, or to the city
again will withdraw, now that they have overcome the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: and what they are devising among themselves, whether they are eager to stay here by the ships, far off, or will withdraw again to the city, now that they have overcome the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: The question goes on. ἅσσα is ‘what things’, and μητιόωσι, with the stretched vowel of epic, is the present of μητιάω ‘devise’. ἢ μεμάασιν ‘or are they eager’ (μεμάασιν, perfect of μέμαα, with the sense of a present) takes the infinitive μένειν ‘to stay’, and ἦε … ἀναχωρήσουσιν ‘or will withdraw’ is the other alternative; πόλιν δέ has the suffix -δε of direction, ‘to the city’. δαμάσαντο is the middle aorist of δαμάζω ‘overcome’, with γε marking the reason. Odysseus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Δόλων Εὐμήδεος υἱός·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe Dolōn Eumēdeos huios·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Dolon, Eumedes’ son:
sentences.i: Then Dolon, the son of Eumedes, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Dolon replies. τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is ‘him then in turn addressed’ (αὖτε ‘in turn, again’), and Δόλων Εὐμήδεος υἱός is the formula that names him, as the poet did when he brought him in (10.314 in the last part).

sentences.t: τοὶ γὰρ ἐγώ τοι ταῦτα μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως καταλέξω.
sentences.tr: toi gar egō toi tauta mal’ atrekeōs katalexō.
sentences.l: “Well then, I to you these things very exactly will recount.
sentences.i: “Well then, I will tell you these things quite exactly.
sentences.n: τοὶ γάρ, printed as two words, is the particle compound τοιγάρ ‘well then’, the Odyssey’s English for the same word in the near-identical 24.303, and the second τοι is the dative ‘to you’. καταλέξω is the future of καταλέγω, picking up Odysseus’ κατάλεξον (405), and μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως ‘very exactly’ gives back his ἀτρεκέως: Dolon promises just what he was asked for.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ μὲν μετὰ τοῖσιν, ὅσοι βουληφόροι εἰσί,
βουλὰς βουλεύει θείου παρὰ σήματι Ἴλου
νόσφιν ἀπὸ φλοίσβου·
sentences.tr:
Hektōr men meta toisin, hosoi boulēphoroi eisi,
boulas bouleuei theiou para sēmati Ilou
nosphin apo phloisbou·
sentences.i: Hector, for his part, is holding counsel with all those who are councillors beside the tomb of divine Ilus, away from the din;
sentences.n: Dolon begins with where Hector is. βουληφόροι is ‘counsel-bearers’, the men of the council, and βουλὰς βουλεύει, ‘takes counsels’, repeats one root in the way English says ‘takes counsel’. παρὰ σήματι is ‘beside the tomb’ (σῆμα is the house ‘tomb’ when it marks a grave), and θείου is the house ‘divine’; Ἴλου is Ilus, whose tomb is the place of the meeting. νόσφιν ἀπὸ φλοίσβου is ‘away from the din’, with φλοῖσβος ‘roar, din’ (of battle or sea). The unit stops at the raised dot in mid-line.

sentences.t:
φυλακὰς δ’ ἃς εἴρεαι ἥρως
οὔ τις κεκριμένη ῥύεται στρατὸν οὐδὲ φυλάσσει.
sentences.tr:
phylakas d’ has eireai hērōs
ou tis kekrimenē rhyetai straton oude phylassei.
sentences.l:
the watches which you ask about, hero,
no one picked-out keeps the army safe, nor keeps watch.
sentences.i: As for the watches you ask about, hero, no watch set apart protects the army or keeps watch.
sentences.n: φυλακὰς … ἃς εἴρεαι puts the thing asked about in 408 first, ‘the watches that you ask about’, and the sentence then goes on as if with a new subject, οὔ τις κεκριμένη ‘no one picked out’, which is feminine and so an unnamed watch. εἴρεαι is ‘you ask’ (epic εἴρομαι, uncontracted), ἥρως is the vocative ‘hero’ (a title of courtesy), and κεκριμένη is the perfect passive participle of κρίνω ‘separate, pick out’. ῥύεται is the middle of ῥύομαι ‘protect’.

sentences.t:
ὅσσαι μὲν Τρώων πυρὸς ἐσχάραι, οἷσιν ἀνάγκη
οἷ δ’ ἐγρηγόρθασι φυλασσέμεναί τε κέλονται
ἀλλήλοις·
sentences.tr:
hossai men Trōōn pyros escharai, hoisin anankē
hoi d’ egrēgorthasi phylassemenai te kelontai
allēlois·
sentences.i: At every one of the Trojans’ hearth-fires, the men who must are awake and bid one another keep watch;
sentences.n: The grammar is loose but the sense is plain. ὅσσαι … πυρὸς ἐσχάραι ‘as many hearths of fire as’ stands first as the topic; οἷσιν ἀνάγκη ‘for whom there is need’ is a relative clause with ἐστί understood (οἷσιν is masculine or neuter, so it points to the men at the fires, not to the feminine ἐσχάραι); and οἳ δ’, ‘and they’, takes up those men. ἐγρηγόρθασι is a perfect of ἐγείρω with the force of a present, ‘are awake’, and κέλονται, from κέλομαι ‘bid’, takes the infinitive φυλασσέμεναι ‘to keep watch’. ἀλλήλοις ‘one another’ opens line 420, and the unit stops after it at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ αὖτε πολύκλητοι ἐπίκουροι
εὕδουσι·
sentences.tr:
atar aute polyklētoi epikouroi
heudousi·
sentences.l:
but in turn the much-summoned allies
are asleep;
sentences.i: but the allies, summoned from many places, are asleep;
sentences.n: ἀτὰρ αὖτε ‘but in turn’ sets the allies against the Trojans. ἐπίκουροι ‘allies’ is the house word, and πολύκλητοι, from πολύς and καλέω ‘summon’, is ‘summoned from many places’ (‘much-summoned’ in the literal layer). εὕδουσι is ‘they sleep’ (εὕδω).

sentences.t: Τρωσὶν γὰρ ἐπιτραπέουσι φυλάσσειν·
sentences.tr: Trōsin gar epitrapeousi phylassein·
sentences.l: for to the Trojans they entrust it, to keep watch;
sentences.i: for they leave the watching to the Trojans;
sentences.n: ἐπιτραπέουσι is ‘they entrust, they leave to’, from ἐπιτρέπω, with the dative Τρωσίν ‘to the Trojans’ and the infinitive φυλάσσειν ‘to keep watch’; the ending -έουσι is an epic form. γάρ gives the reason the allies sleep.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ σφιν παῖδες σχεδὸν εἵαται οὐδὲ γυναῖκες.
sentences.tr: ou gar sphin paides schedon heiatai oude gynaikes.
sentences.l: For not near them are seated children, nor wives.”
sentences.i: For their children and wives are not sitting near them.”
sentences.n: σφιν is ‘to them’ and must mean the allies, since the point is that they have no families at hand; the Greek leaves the rest to be understood. εἵαται is the Ionic third plural of ἧμαι ‘sit, be posted’, ‘are seated’, and σχεδόν is ‘near’. Dolon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. The reply formula τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη is ‘him answering addressed’ (ἀπαμειβόμενος from ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’), with πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’. The line stands in the last part at 10.382 and takes its English.

sentences.t:
πῶς γὰρ νῦν Τρώεσσι μεμιγμένοι ἱπποδάμοισιν
εὕδουσ’ ἦ ἀπάνευθε;
sentences.tr:
pōs gar nyn Trōessi memigmenoi hippodamoisin
heudous’ ē apaneuthe;
sentences.l:
“For how now, mingled with the horse-taming Trojans,
are they sleeping, or apart?
sentences.i: “For how are they sleeping now: mixed in with the Trojans, tamers of horses, or apart?
sentences.n: πῶς γάρ ‘for how?’ takes up what Dolon has just said, that the allies sleep (421); the subject of εὕδουσ’ ‘they sleep’ is those allies. μεμιγμένοι is the perfect passive participle of μίγνυμι ‘mix’, here ‘mingled’ with a dative, and ἱπποδάμοισιν is the stock ‘horse-taming’ of the Trojans. ἦ is ‘or’ here, setting ἀπάνευθε ‘apart’ against the first alternative, and the question ends at the mid-line question mark after ἀπάνευθε.

sentences.t: δίειπέ μοι ὄφρα δαείω.
sentences.tr: dieipe moi ophra daeiō.
sentences.l: Tell it through to me, that I may learn.”
sentences.i: Tell me all of it, so that I may learn.”
sentences.n: δίειπε is the aorist imperative of διεῖπον ‘tell right through, tell in full’, and μοι ‘to me’. δαείω is a subjunctive of δάω, whose passive-shaped aorist means ‘learn’, after ὄφρα ‘so that’. Odysseus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Δόλων Εὐμήδεος υἱός·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Dolōn Eumēdeos huios·
sentences.l: Him then answered Dolon, Eumedes’ son:
sentences.i: Then Dolon, the son of Eumedes, answered him:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. This is the reply formula with ἠμείβετο ‘answered’ (kept apart from the αὖτε προσέειπε ‘addressed in turn’ of 412), ending in the same name-phrase for Dolon.

sentences.t: τοὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ καὶ ταῦτα μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως καταλέξω.
sentences.tr: toi gar egō kai tauta mal’ atrekeōs katalexō.
sentences.l: “Well then, I these things also very exactly will recount.
sentences.i: “Well then, I will tell these things too, quite exactly.
sentences.n: Nearly a repeat of 413: τοὶ γάρ is again ‘well then’, but there is no second τοι here, and καί ‘also’ stands before ταῦτα ‘these things’, the new matter being where each people lies.

sentences.t:
πρὸς μὲν ἁλὸς Κᾶρες καὶ Παίονες ἀγκυλότοξοι
καὶ Λέλεγες καὶ Καύκωνες δῖοί τε Πελασγοί,
πρὸς Θύμβρης δ’ ἔλαχον Λύκιοι Μυσοί τ’ ἀγέρωχοι
καὶ Φρύγες ἱππόμαχοι καὶ Μῄονες ἱπποκορυσταί.
sentences.tr:
pros men halos Kares kai Paiones ankylotoxoi
kai Leleges kai Kaukōnes dioi te Pelasgoi,
pros Thymbrēs d’ elachon Lykioi Mysoi t’ agerōchoi
kai Phryges hippomachoi kai Mēiones hippokorystai.
sentences.l:
Toward the sea are Carians and Paeonians of the curved bows
and Leleges and Caucones and heavenly Pelasgians,
and toward Thymbre obtained by lot Lycians and lofty Mysians
and horse-fighting Phrygians and horse-arming Maeonians.
sentences.i: Toward the sea are the Carians, the Paeonians with their curved bows, the Leleges, the Caucones and the heavenly Pelasgians; and toward Thymbre the Lycians have received their place by lot, with the lofty Mysians, the horse-fighting Phrygians and the Maeonians, armed with horses.
sentences.n: A catalogue of the allies by where they lie: πρὸς ἁλός ‘toward the sea’ and πρὸς Θύμβρης ‘toward Thymbre’, a place name. The peoples are Κᾶρες Carians, Παίονες Paeonians, Λέλεγες, Καύκωνες, Πελασγοί, Λύκιοι Lycians, Μυσοί Mysians, Φρύγες Phrygians and Μῄονες Maeonians; δῖοι is the house ‘heavenly’. ἀγκυλότοξοι is ‘of the curved bows’. ἔλαχον is the aorist of λαγχάνω ‘obtain by lot’, here ‘received their place by lot’. ἀγέρωχοι, ‘lofty’, is a word whose meaning is not known. ἱππόμαχοι is ‘horse-fighting’, and the Greek does not say whether on horseback or from chariots. ἱπποκορυσταί is ‘horse-arming’, ‘armed with horses’; whether this is chariot-fighters or horsehair crests is not known.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τί ἢ ἐμὲ ταῦτα διεξερέεσθε ἕκαστα;
sentences.tr: alla ti ē eme tauta diexereesthe hekasta;
sentences.l: But why then do you question me through about these things, each one?
sentences.i: But why do you question me about each of these things?
sentences.n: Dolon turns on his questioners. The edition prints ἢ, which is the word for ‘or’, but no ‘or’ fits here; it is read as the emphatic particle ἦ, ‘then, really’. διεξερέεσθε is the present of διεξερέομαι ‘question closely’ with the epic uncontracted ending, a plural said to the two men, and ἕκαστα is ‘each thing’, a neuter plural.

sentences.t:
εἰ γὰρ δὴ μέματον Τρώων καταδῦναι ὅμιλον
Θρήϊκες οἷδ’ ἀπάνευθε νεήλυδες ἔσχατοι ἄλλων·
sentences.tr:
ei gar dē mematon Trōōn katadynai homilon
Thrēïkes hoid’ apaneuthe neēlydes eschatoi allōn·
sentences.l:
For if indeed you two are eager to enter the throng of the Trojans,
there are these Thracians, apart, newcomers, last of the others;
sentences.i: If you two are really eager to enter the throng of the Trojans, here are these Thracians, apart, new arrivals, the last of the others;
sentences.n: The sentence gives its condition and leaves the main clause to be understood: ‘if you want a way into the Trojan host — here are the Thracians’. εἰ γάρ here is ‘for if’, with an indicative, not the ‘if only’ of a wish. μέματον is the dual of μέμαα ‘be eager’, ‘you two are eager’; καταδῦναι is the aorist infinitive of καταδύω ‘go down into’; Θρήϊκες οἷδ’ is ‘these Thracians’ (οἷδε, ‘these here’); νεήλυδες is ‘newly come’; ἔσχατοι ἄλλων ‘last of the others’ puts them at the edge.

sentences.t: ἐν δέ σφιν Ῥῆσος βασιλεὺς πάϊς Ἠϊονῆος.
sentences.tr: en de sphin Rhēsos basileus païs Ēïonēos.
sentences.l: And among them Rhesus the king, the son of Eioneus.
sentences.i: And among them is Rhesus, their king, the son of Eioneus.
sentences.n: ἐν δέ σφιν is ‘and among them’ (the Thracians); there is no verb, ‘is’ being understood. Ῥῆσος is Rhesus, βασιλεύς ‘king’, and πάϊς Ἠϊονῆος ‘son of Eioneus’, with πάϊς the epic form of παῖς and Ἠϊονῆος the epic genitive in -ῆος.

sentences.t: τοῦ δὴ καλλίστους ἵππους ἴδον ἠδὲ μεγίστους·
sentences.tr: tou dē kallistous hippous idon ēde megistous·
sentences.l: His horses I saw, the fairest and the greatest;
sentences.i: I saw his horses: the fairest and the largest.
sentences.n: τοῦ δή is ‘of him, indeed’, and τοῦ ‘his’ is the pronoun. καλλίστους ‘fairest’ and μεγίστους ‘greatest’ (of horses, ‘largest’) are superlatives. ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω, ‘I saw’.

sentences.t: λευκότεροι χιόνος, θείειν δ’ ἀνέμοισιν ὁμοῖοι·
sentences.tr: leukoteroi chionos, theiein d’ anemoisin homoioi·
sentences.l: whiter than snow, and in running like the winds;
sentences.i: whiter than snow, and for running like the winds;
sentences.n: λευκότεροι is a comparative, ‘whiter’, with the genitive of comparison χιόνος ‘than snow’. θείειν is the epic infinitive of θέω ‘run’, saying in what respect: ‘like the winds in running’. ἀνέμοισιν is the dative plural of ἄνεμος ‘wind’.

sentences.t: ἅρμα δέ οἱ χρυσῷ τε καὶ ἀργύρῳ εὖ ἤσκηται·
sentences.tr: harma de hoi chrysōi te kai argyrōi eu ēskētai·
sentences.l: and his chariot with gold and with silver is well wrought;
sentences.i: his chariot is finely worked with gold and silver;
sentences.n: ἤσκηται is the perfect passive of ἀσκέω ‘work with skill, fashion’, ‘has been wrought’, with the datives χρυσῷ τε καὶ ἀργύρῳ ‘with gold and with silver’ and εὖ ‘well’. οἱ is the dative ‘his’. Here ἅρμα is singular; in 393 the plural ἅρματα stood for one chariot as well.

sentences.t:
τεύχεα δὲ χρύσεια πελώρια θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι
ἤλυθ’ ἔχων·
sentences.tr:
teuchea de chryseia pelōria thauma idesthai
ēlyth’ echōn·
sentences.l:
and armour of gold, huge, a wonder to behold,
he has come bringing;
sentences.i: And he has come with golden armour, huge, a wonder to look at;
sentences.n: τεύχεα is the house ‘armour’, kept apart from ἔντεα ‘gear’, and it is the object of ἔχων ‘having, bringing’. ἤλυθε is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι (= Attic ἦλθε). χρύσεια is ‘golden’, πελώρια ‘huge’, and θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι ‘a wonder to behold’, with ἰδέσθαι the aorist infinitive of ὁράω saying in what respect. The unit stops at the raised dot in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὰ μὲν οὔ τι καταθνητοῖσιν ἔοικεν
ἄνδρεσσιν φορέειν, ἀλλ’ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν.
sentences.tr:
ta men ou ti katathnētoisin eoiken
andressin phoreein, all’ athanatoisi theoisin.
sentences.l:
these are in no way fitting for those liable to death,
men, to wear, but for the immortal gods.
sentences.i: such armour is in no way fitting for men who are liable to death to wear, but for the immortal gods.
sentences.n: τά picks up τεύχεα ‘armour’ and μέν sets up the contrast with ἀλλά. ἔοικεν, with a dative and an infinitive, is ‘is fitting for … to …’. καταθνητοῖσιν ἄνδρεσσιν is ‘men liable to death’ (καταθνητός, the house word), in the epic dative -εσσιν, and φορέειν is the uncontracted infinitive of φορέω ‘wear, bear’. ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν is the stock opposite, the immortal gods.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ μὲν νῦν νηυσὶ πελάσσετον ὠκυπόροισιν,
ἠέ με δήσαντες λίπετ’ αὐτόθι νηλέϊ δεσμῷ,
ὄφρά κεν ἔλθητον καὶ πειρηθῆτον ἐμεῖο
ἠὲ κατ’ αἶσαν ἔειπον ἐν ὑμῖν, ἦε καὶ οὐκί.
sentences.tr:
all’ eme men nyn nēusi pelasseton ōkyporoisin,
ēe me dēsantes lipet’ autothi nēleï desmōi,
ophra ken elthēton kai peirēthēton emeio
ēe kat’ aisan eeipon en hymin, ēe kai ouki.
sentences.l:
But me now to the ships, the swift-faring, bring near, you two,
or bind me and leave me here in a pitiless bond,
until you two come and make trial of me,
whether in due measure I spoke among you, or not.”
sentences.i: But as for me, bring me now to the swift-faring ships, or else bind me and leave me here in a pitiless bond, until you two have come and made trial of me, to see whether I spoke in due measure among you, or not.”
sentences.n: Dolon’s offer has two halves joined by ἠέ ‘or’: take me to the ships, or bind me here. πελάσσετον is a dual, ‘you two’, in the form of the future (the aorist subjunctive has the same shape) of πελάζω ‘bring near’, used as a command; λίπετ’ (λίπετε) and δήσαντες are plurals, so the speaker slides from the dual to the plural, though he means the two men. νηλέϊ δεσμῷ is ‘in a pitiless bond’ (νηλεής is the house ‘pitiless’), and αὐτόθι is ‘right here’. ἔλθητον and πειρηθῆτον are dual aorist subjunctives after ὄφρα κεν, which could also be ‘so that you may come’; πειράω takes the genitive, and ἐμεῖο is the epic ‘of me’. κατ’ αἶσαν ἔειπον is ‘I spoke in due measure’, with ἔειπον the aorist of εἶπον with its epic doubled vowel; ἦε καὶ οὐκί is ‘or not’, οὐκί being a strengthened οὐ. Dolon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ar’ hypodra idōn prosephē krateros Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed strong Diomedes:
sentences.i: Then strong Diomedes, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Diomedes replies. This is the formula for an answer given with a dark look, which the Iliad has at 4.411 and the Odyssey for Odysseus at 8.165. ὑπόδρα is an adverb, ‘from under (the brows)’, ‘with a scowl’; its derivation is not certain. κρατερός is the house ‘strong’.

sentences.t: μὴ δή μοι φύξίν γε Δόλων ἐμβάλλεο θυμῷ·
sentences.tr: mē dē moi phyxin ge Dolōn emballeo thymōi·
sentences.l: “Do not now, for me, flight, Dolon, put into your heart;
sentences.i: “Do not, I tell you, Dolon, put thoughts of flight into your heart;
sentences.n: Diomedes cuts off Dolon’s hope before it forms. μὴ δή with the present imperative ἐμβάλλεο (the middle of ἐμβάλλω ‘put in’, with the epic ending -εο for -ου) is a prohibition, and φύξιν ‘flight, escape’ is its object, θυμῷ ‘in your heart’ the place. μοι is an ethic dative, ‘as far as I am concerned’, which English carries as ‘I tell you’; γε stresses φύξιν; Δόλων is the vocative.

sentences.t: ἐσθλά περ ἀγγείλας, ἐπεὶ ἵκεο χεῖρας ἐς ἁμάς.
sentences.tr: esthla per angeilas, epei hikeo cheiras es hamas.
sentences.l: though good things you have reported, since you have come to our hands.
sentences.i: though what you have reported is good, since you have come into our hands.
sentences.n: ἐσθλά περ ἀγγείλας is ‘although you reported good things’, περ making the participle concessive, and ἀγγείλας is the aorist participle of ἀγγέλλω. ἵκεο is the aorist middle of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’, ‘you came’, with no augment, and ἁμάς is a by-form of ἡμετέρας ‘our’: ‘into our hands’, where one is in another’s power. The clause hangs on the prohibition before it.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν γάρ κέ σε νῦν ἀπολύσομεν ἠὲ μεθῶμεν,
ἦ τε καὶ ὕστερον εἶσθα θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
ἠὲ διοπτεύσων ἢ ἐναντίβιον πολεμίξων·
sentences.tr:
ei men gar ke se nyn apolysomen ēe methōmen,
ē te kai hysteron eistha thoas epi nēas Achaiōn
ēe diopteusōn ē enantibion polemixōn·
sentences.i: For if we release you now, or let you go, you will surely come later to the swift ships of the Achaeans too, either to spy them out or to fight us head-on;
sentences.n: Diomedes’ reasoning, first half. εἰ … κε with ἀπολύσομεν and μεθῶμεν is ‘if we should release, or let go’; ἀπολύσομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive (or future) of ἀπολύω, and μεθῶμεν the aorist subjunctive of μεθίημι ‘let go’. ἦ τε καί is ‘surely also’, and εἶσθα is the second singular of εἶμι ‘go, come’, with the sense of a future. διοπτεύσων ‘to spy’ and πολεμίξων ‘to fight’ are future participles of purpose, and ἐναντίβιον is the house ‘head-on’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κ’ ἐμῇς ὑπὸ χερσὶ δαμεὶς ἀπὸ θυμὸν ὀλέσσῃς,
οὐκέτ’ ἔπειτα σὺ πῆμά ποτ’ ἔσσεαι Ἀργείοισιν.
sentences.tr:
ei de k’ emēis hypo chersi dameis apo thymon olessēis,
ouket’ epeita sy pēma pot’ esseai Argeioisin.
sentences.l:
but if, overcome beneath my hands, you lose your life,
no longer after that will you ever be a woe to the Argives.”
sentences.i: but if, overcome beneath my hands, you lose your life, you will never again be a woe to the Argives.”
sentences.n: The second half answers the first, εἰ μέν … εἰ δέ. δαμείς is the aorist passive participle of δαμάζω ‘overcome’, and ἀπὸ … ὀλέσσῃς is a tmesis for ἀπολέσσῃς, ‘you lose’, with θυμόν ‘life’, the house reading when the θυμός leaves the body. οὐκέτ’ ἔπειτα is ‘no longer after that’, ἔσσεαι the epic future ‘you will be’, and πῆμα the house ‘woe’. Ἀργείοισιν is one of the three names for the army, kept as ‘Argives’. Diomedes’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ, καὶ ὃ μέν μιν ἔμελλε γενείου χειρὶ παχείῃ
ἁψάμενος λίσσεσθαι, ὃ δ’ αὐχένα μέσσον ἔλασσε
φασγάνῳ ἀΐξας, ἀπὸ δ’ ἄμφω κέρσε τένοντε·
sentences.tr:
ē, kai ho men min emelle geneiou cheiri pacheiēi
hapsamenos lissesthai, ho d’ auchena messon elasse
phasganōi aïxas, apo d’ amphō kerse tenonte·
sentences.i: So he said, and Dolon was just about to touch him by the chin with his thick hand and plead with him, but Diomedes darted at him and struck the middle of his neck with the sword, and cut through both tendons;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ἦ, καί is ‘he spoke, and’. ὃ μέν … ὃ δ’ is ‘the one … the other’, Dolon and Diomedes; the Greek names neither. ἔμελλε takes the infinitive λίσσεσθαι ‘to beg’, and ἁψάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἅπτω ‘touch’ with the genitive γενείου ‘by the chin’; to touch the chin is a suppliant’s gesture. χειρὶ παχείῃ is ‘with a thick hand’, ἔλασσε the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘strike’, and ἀΐξας the house ‘darting’. ἀπὸ … κέρσε is a tmesis, ‘cut off’, and τένοντε is a dual, ‘the two tendons’, agreeing with ἄμφω ‘both’.

sentences.t: φθεγγομένου δ’ ἄρα τοῦ γε κάρη κονίῃσιν ἐμίχθη.
sentences.tr: phthengomenou d’ ara tou ge karē koniēisin emichthē.
sentences.l: And as he was speaking, then, his head in the dust was mingled.
sentences.i: As he was speaking, his head was mingled with the dust.
sentences.n: This line is also Odyssey 22.329 and takes that English. φθεγγομένου τοῦ γε is a genitive absolute, ‘he speaking’: Dolon is still speaking as the blow falls. κάρη is ‘head’, κονίῃσιν the dative plural of κονία ‘dust’ (a plural for the one dust), and ἐμίχθη the aorist passive of μίγνυμι ‘mix’; the Greek says ‘mingled’, not ‘rolled’.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἀπὸ μὲν κτιδέην κυνέην κεφαλῆφιν ἕλοντο
καὶ λυκέην καὶ τόξα παλίντονα καὶ δόρυ μακρόν·
sentences.tr:
tou d’ apo men ktideēn kyneēn kephalēphin helonto
kai lykeēn kai toxa palintona kai dory makron·
sentences.l:
And from him off the weasel-skin helmet from his head they took,
and the wolfskin, and the back-stretched bow, and the long spear;
sentences.i: They took from him the weasel-skin helmet from his head, and the wolfskin, the back-stretched bow and the long spear;
sentences.n: The two spies strip the body; their names are not given, and ἕλοντο is a plural. τοῦ … ἀπὸ … ἕλοντο is a tmesis, ‘took off from him’. κτιδέην κυνέην is the weasel-skin helmet that Dolon put on at 10.335, and λυκέην ‘wolfskin’ the grey wolf’s hide he wore at 10.334, an adjective standing alone for its noun. κεφαλῆφιν is ‘from the head’, with the ending -φιν. τόξα παλίντονα is ‘the back-stretched bow’, a plural for one bow, and δόρυ μακρόν ‘the long spear’.

sentences.t:
καὶ τά γ’ Ἀθηναίῃ ληΐτιδι δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ὑψόσ’ ἀνέσχεθε χειρὶ καὶ εὐχόμενος ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.tr:
kai ta g’ Athēnaiēi lēïtidi dios Odysseus
hypsos’ aneschethe cheiri kai euchomenos epos ēuda·
sentences.l:
And these things to Athena, the spoil-giving, heavenly Odysseus
high held up in his hand, and praying spoke a word:
sentences.i: And heavenly Odysseus held these up high in his hand to Athena, giver of spoil, and said, praying:
sentences.n: Odysseus dedicates the spoils. τά γε is ‘these things’, the spoils of 458–459, and Ἀθηναίῃ ληΐτιδι is the dative ‘to Athena’ with her epithet ληΐτις, from ληΐς ‘booty’; that she is the giver of booty, rather than its keeper, is the usual explanation and not certain. ἀνέσχεθε is ‘held up’ (ἀνέχω), ὑψόσ’ is ὑψόσε ‘on high’, and εὐχόμενος is ‘praying’ here, a prayer to a goddess. ἔπος ηὔδα is ‘spoke a word’ (ηὔδα, imperfect of αὐδάω), and δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is the house ‘heavenly Odysseus’.

sentences.t: χαῖρε θεὰ τοῖσδεσσι·
sentences.tr: chaire thea toisdessi·
sentences.l: “Be glad, goddess, in these;
sentences.i: “Be glad of these, goddess;
sentences.n: The prayer opens with χαῖρε, the imperative of χαίρω ‘be glad’; with the dative τοῖσδεσσι (the epic form of τοῖσδε ‘these’) it means ‘be glad of these’, the gifts, and is not the greeting ‘Welcome’ that the house gives χαῖρε when it greets a person. θεά is ‘goddess’, Athena. The unit stops at the raised dot in mid-line.

sentences.t:
σὲ γὰρ πρώτην ἐν Ὀλύμπῳ
πάντων ἀθανάτων ἐπιδωσόμεθ’·
sentences.tr:
se gar prōtēn en Olympōi
pantōn athanatōn epidōsometh’·
sentences.l:
for you first on Olympus
of all the immortals we shall give to;
sentences.i: for it is you we shall make our offerings to, first of all the immortals on Olympus;
sentences.n: ἐπιδωσόμεθ’ is the future middle of ἐπιδίδωμι, ‘give in addition, give over’, and with a person in the accusative (σέ ‘you’) its sense is not secure: ‘make offerings to’ is what the context gives, the spoils just held up being the gift. σὲ … πρώτην ‘you first’ and πάντων ἀθανάτων ‘of all the immortals’ put Athena at the head of the gods who will be honoured; ἐν Ὀλύμπῳ is ‘on Olympus’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ αὖτις
πέμψον ἐπὶ Θρῃκῶν ἀνδρῶν ἵππους τε καὶ εὐνάς.
sentences.tr:
alla kai autis
pempson epi Thrēikōn andrōn hippous te kai eunas.
sentences.l:
but also again
send us to the Thracian men’s horses and beds.”
sentences.i: but send us on again to the horses and the sleeping-places of the Thracian men.”
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ αὖτις is ‘but also again, once more’. πέμψον is the aorist imperative of πέμπω ‘send’, with no object stated (‘send us’). ἐπί with the accusative is ‘to’, and Θρῃκῶν ἀνδρῶν ‘of Thracian men’ goes with ἵππους τε καὶ εὐνάς ‘horses and beds’, εὐναί being the sleeping-places as in 408. The prayer, and Odysseus’ speech, end here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν, καὶ ἀπὸ ἕθεν ὑψόσ’ ἀείρας
θῆκεν ἀνὰ μυρίκην·
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephōnēsen, kai apo hethen hypsos’ aeiras
thēken ana myrikēn·
sentences.l:
So then he spoke, and from himself high raising
he set them on a tamarisk;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and, raising the spoils high, away from himself, set them up on a tamarisk;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν is ‘so then he spoke’ (ἐφώνησεν, aorist of φωνέω ‘speak’). ἀπὸ ἕθεν is ‘away from himself’, ἕθεν being the old third-person pronoun, and ἀείρας the aorist participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’; the object, the spoils, is understood. ἀνὰ μυρίκην is ‘up on a tamarisk’, μυρίκη being a shrub. Line 466 is metrically irregular as the scansion table reads it, at ἀνὰ μυρίκην: the final α of ἀνά is short and has to be lengthened before μ, and the υ of μυρίκην, which the table counts long, has to be read short.

sentences.t:
δέελον δ’ ἐπὶ σῆμά τ’ ἔθηκε
συμμάρψας δόνακας μυρίκης τ’ ἐριθηλέας ὄζους,
μὴ λάθοι αὖτις ἰόντε θοὴν διὰ νύκτα μέλαιναν.
sentences.tr:
deelon d’ epi sēma t’ ethēke
symmarpsas donakas myrikēs t’ erithēleas ozous,
mē lathoi autis ionte thoēn dia nykta melainan.
sentences.l:
and a conspicuous sign upon it he set,
gathering reeds and the luxuriant boughs of tamarisk,
so that it should not escape them going again through the swift black night.
sentences.i: and he set a conspicuous sign upon it, gathering reeds and the luxuriant boughs of the tamarisk, so that it would not escape the two of them when they came back through the swift black night.
sentences.n: δέελον is an adjective, ‘plain to see’, a rare word whose sense is taken from the context; it qualifies σῆμα ‘sign’, and ἐπὶ … ἔθηκε is a tmesis, ‘set upon (it)’. συμμάρψας is the aorist participle of συμμάρπτω ‘grasp together, gather up’; δόνακας ‘reeds’ and ὄζους ‘boughs’ are its objects, and ἐριθηλέας is ‘luxuriant’. μὴ λάθοι is an aorist optative of λανθάνω ‘escape the notice of’, ‘lest it escape’, in a purpose clause; ἰόντε is a dual participle, ‘the two going’, and θοὴν … νύκτα μέλαιναν is the same ‘swift black night’ as in 394. Line 467 is metrically irregular as the scansion table reads it, at μυρίκης, where the υ, which the table counts long, has to be read short, as in 466.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ βάτην προτέρω διά τ’ ἔντεα καὶ μέλαν αἷμα,
αἶψα δ’ ἐπὶ Θρῃκῶν ἀνδρῶν τέλος ἷξον ἰόντες.
sentences.tr:
tō de batēn proterō dia t’ entea kai melan haima,
aipsa d’ epi Thrēikōn andrōn telos hixon iontes.
sentences.l:
And the two went farther, through gear and black blood,
and quickly to the company of the Thracian men they came, going.
sentences.i: The two went on, through the gear and the black blood, and quickly, as they went, reached the company of the Thracian men.
sentences.n: τώ is the dual of the pronoun, ‘the two’, and βάτην the dual aorist of βαίνω, with no augment; προτέρω is ‘farther on’. διά τ’ ἔντεα καὶ μέλαν αἷμα, ‘through gear and black blood’, is the line-end of 10.298, where they set out. αἶψα is ‘quickly’, and τέλος here is ‘company, body of men’ and not ‘end’. ἷξον is an unaugmented aorist of ἵκω ‘reached’, plural although the subject is two; ἰόντες is ‘going’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ εὗδον καμάτῳ ἀδηκότες, ἔντεα δέ σφιν
καλὰ παρ’ αὐτοῖσι χθονὶ κέκλιτο εὖ κατὰ κόσμον
τριστοιχί·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ heudon kamatōi adēkotes, entea de sphin
kala par’ autoisi chthoni keklito eu kata kosmon
tristoichi·
sentences.i: They were asleep, worn out with weariness, and their fine gear lay on the ground beside them in good order, in three rows;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, the Thracians. εὗδον is the imperfect of εὕδω ‘sleep’, and ἀδηκότες is the house ‘worn out’, as at 399 (the sense is not quite certain), with καμάτῳ ‘with weariness’. ἔντεα is the house ‘gear’, and κέκλιτο the pluperfect passive of κλίνω, ‘lay, was laid’. σφιν is ‘for them’, and αὐτοῖσι ‘themselves’ after παρά, ‘beside them’. εὖ κατὰ κόσμον is ‘well in due order’, and τριστοιχί, an adverb, ‘in three rows’. The unit stops at the raised dot in mid-line.

sentences.t: παρὰ δέ σφιν ἑκάστῳ δίζυγες ἵπποι.
sentences.tr: para de sphin hekastōi dizyges hippoi.
sentences.l: and beside each one of them a yoked pair of horses.
sentences.i: and beside each man a yoked pair of horses.
sentences.n: δίζυγες is ‘yoked in a pair’, with ἵπποι ‘horses’; ἑκάστῳ is ‘each one’, a dative, and σφιν ‘them’. ‘Were’ is understood.

sentences.t:
Ῥῆσος δ’ ἐν μέσῳ εὗδε, παρ’ αὐτῷ δ’ ὠκέες ἵπποι
ἐξ ἐπιδιφριάδος πυμάτης ἱμᾶσι δέδεντο.
sentences.tr:
Rhēsos d’ en mesōi heude, par’ autōi d’ ōkees hippoi
ex epidiphriados pymatēs himasi dedento.
sentences.l:
And Rhesus in the middle was sleeping, and beside him the swift horses
from the outermost chariot-rail with straps were tied.
sentences.i: Rhesus was sleeping in the middle, and beside him his swift horses were tied with straps to the outermost chariot-rail.
sentences.n: Rhesus, named last at 435, sleeps ἐν μέσῳ ‘in the middle’ of his men, and ὠκέες ἵπποι is the house ‘swift horses’. ἐπιδιφριάς is a rare word for a part of the chariot, the ‘chariot-rail’; which part is not certain. πυμάτης is ‘outermost, last’. ἱμᾶσι is the dative plural of ἱμάς ‘strap’, and δέδεντο the pluperfect passive of δέω ‘bind’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς προπάροιθεν ἰδὼν Διομήδεϊ δεῖξεν·
sentences.tr: ton d’ Odyseus proparoithen idōn Diomēdeï deixen·
sentences.l: Him Odysseus, having seen ahead, to Diomedes showed:
sentences.i: Odysseus saw him ahead and pointed him out to Diomedes:
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’, Rhesus. προπάροιθεν is ‘in front, ahead’, and ἰδών ‘having seen’. Ὀδυσεύς has a single σ here (the metre), against Ὀδυσσεύς in other lines. δεῖξεν is the aorist of δείκνυμι ‘show’, and Διομήδεϊ the epic dative.

sentences.t:
οὗτός τοι Διόμηδες ἀνήρ, οὗτοι δέ τοι ἵπποι,
οὓς νῶϊν πίφαυσκε Δόλων ὃν ἐπέφνομεν ἡμεῖς.
sentences.tr:
houtos toi Diomēdes anēr, houtoi de toi hippoi,
hous nōïn piphauske Dolōn hon epephnomen hēmeis.
sentences.l:
“This, Diomedes, is the man, and these are the horses
which to us two made known Dolon, whom we killed.
sentences.i: “Here, Diomedes, is the man, and here are the horses that Dolon made known to us, Dolon whom we killed.
sentences.n: οὗτός τοι … οὗτοι δέ τοι: the two τοι are the particle ‘you see’, and the two demonstratives ‘this one’, ‘these’ are the pointing. νῶϊν is the dual dative of ἐγώ, ‘to us two’. πίφαυσκε is the imperfect of πιφαύσκω ‘make known’, with no augment; Dolon made the horses known in 435–437. ἐπέφνομεν is an old aorist of φένω ‘kill’, with ἡμεῖς ‘we ourselves’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ πρόφερε κρατερὸν μένος·
sentences.tr: all’ age dē prophere krateron menos·
sentences.l: But come now, bring forward strong might;
sentences.i: But come now, put forth your strong might;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is ‘but come now’ (compare 405). πρόφερε is the present imperative of προφέρω ‘bring forward, put forth’, and κρατερὸν μένος ‘strong might’ is the house phrase. The unit stops at the raised dot in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί σε χρὴ
ἑστάμεναι μέλεον σὺν τεύχεσιν, ἀλλὰ λύ’ ἵππους·
sentences.tr:
oude ti se chrē
hestamenai meleon syn teuchesin, alla ly’ hippous·
sentences.l:
and in no way is it needful for you
to stand idle in your armour, but loose the horses;
sentences.i: and there is no need for you to stand idle in your armour: loose the horses;
sentences.n: οὐδέ τί σε χρή is ‘and there is no need at all for you’, with ἑστάμεναι the infinitive of ἵστημι ‘stand’ (-μεναι). μέλεον is ‘idly, to no purpose’; elsewhere the adjective means ‘wretched’. σὺν τεύχεσιν is ‘in your armour’, and λύ’ is λῦε with the final vowel dropped, the imperative of λύω ‘loose’: the horses are tied by straps (475).

sentences.t: ἠὲ σύ γ’ ἄνδρας ἔναιρε, μελήσουσιν δ’ ἐμοὶ ἵπποι.
sentences.tr: ēe sy g’ andras enaire, melēsousin d’ emoi hippoi.
sentences.l: or else you kill the men, and the horses will be a care to me.”
sentences.i: or else you kill the men, and the horses will be my concern.”
sentences.n: ἠέ is ‘or else’, offering the other course. ἔναιρε is the present imperative of ἐναίρω ‘kill’, σύ γε ‘you, for your part’, and μελήσουσιν the future of μέλω, ‘will be a care to’, with the dative ἐμοί and the horses as its subject. Odysseus’ speech ends here.
